transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood CSM), Lena Ortiz (Lead ML Eng, Meridian), Rajesh Menon (Platform Eng), Maya Chu (CTO), Tom Becker (DevOps)

Summary note: hands-on run through of SDK quickstart, auth options, and a short discussion about Optimize recommendations for their conversational agent use case.

[00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Maya Chu: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Samira Patel: Great. Quick agenda: Ethan will open with the SDK install and local quickstart, then we’ll cover auth patterns, Diego will touch on security and entitlements, and we’ll wrap with next steps and a pilot plan. Sound good?
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: Yep, good. We mostly want to see the typical dev flow — prod-like auth, how to set up envs and anything Optimize recommends for cost.
[00:24] Ethan Cole: Awesome. I’m gonna share my screen, just a heads up, I’ll be toggling between the Python and TS examples.
[00:30] [screen share starts, minor background noise]
[00:35] Ethan Cole: Alright, in the repo — quickstart — we have two folders. Python first: pip install redwood-inference (note: pip name is example, sometimes transcriber shows red wood or redroom).
[00:50] Tom Becker: Is that the hosted SDK or the dedicated client?
[00:53] Ethan Cole: Good call, that’s the hosted SDK which calls the Redwood API. For Dedicated or Private deployments you'd just point the sdk to your private endpoint and swap credentials. I’ll show the env var pattern shortly.
[01:07] [01:10] Rajesh Menon: And does the SDK handle streaming and chunked responses?
[01:13] Ethan Cole: Yep, we support streaming in both Python and TS. The Python sample uses a streaming iterator; TS has an async event emitter sample. There's a small typo in the example readme where 'stream' is spelled as 'strem' in one place - we’ll fix that.
[01:27] Samira Patel: Quick note: we put a short deck in the follow-up email, and Ethan will link the quickstart repo.
[01:33] Ethan Cole: Back to auth — two common patterns we see: API keys for dev/sandbox and SSO (SAML/OIDC) for staging/prod with role-based access. Demoing API key flow now: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, run the quickstart and you’ll see a sample response.
[01:50] [01:52] Lena Ortiz: For us we need SSO but also token rotation and least privilege. Do you support short lived tokens?
[01:57] Ethan Cole: Yes — short-lived tokens with our credential exchange and recommended refresh pattern, or you can integrate with your KMS/HSM for private deployments. Our docs show a sample with OAuth exchange; we sometimes call that Redwood Token Service in the docs but the transcription sometimes mangles that to 'Redwood Tea Service' — ignore that.
[02:15] [02:17] Rajesh Menon: Any sample for SSO mapping to RBAC? We have groups mapped in Okta, want those mapped to model access.
[02:23] Diego Morales: We have a template mapping for Okta groups to Redwood roles in the security guide — link in the follow-up. It’s a basic claim mapping where group X -> role dev, group Y -> role infra.
[02:36] Maya Chu: Do you enforce audit logs for prompt/response? We need PII auditability.
[02:41] Diego Morales: Yes — audit logs can be routed to your SIEM. For hosted we keep full request/response logs for configurable retention; for Private we offer local log forwarding and can disable request storing if required. There was a slight transcribe earlier that said 'disable resting' — it's 'request storing'.
[02:56] Ethan Cole: Back to env setup. For sandbox we recommend a small local env .env with REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_ENDPOINT=https://api.redwood.ai (example). For Private you point to your private control plane e.g. https://private.redwood.company.local. The TS example uses dotenv; Python uses pydantic settings.
[03:20] [03:22] Tom Becker: Network footprint — what egress do you expect? We can't have broad egress rules.
[03:26] Ethan Cole: Good question. For hosted we recommend egress to a small set of IP ranges we provide; we also support peered VPC for Dedicated which greatly reduces egress concerns. We'll provide the IP CIDR list in the security doc — I’ll put that in the follow-up.
[03:40] [03:42] Lena Ortiz: On the Optimize side, how do we reduce tokens and keep latency consistent?
[03:46] Ethan Cole: Two levers: prefix/KV caching and batching. For retrieval-heavy flows, prefix caching avoids re-computing initial context; for high TPS, smart batching reduces per-token cost but can add small tail latency. There's a tradeoff: we can show an Optimize profile that suggests batch size 8 for your median request length given your traffic sample.
[04:08] [04:10] Rajesh Menon: Do you have automated suggestions? We don't want manual tuning every week.
[04:14] Ethan Cole: Yes, Redwood Optimize offers automated suggestions and will flag regressions. For pilot we can run our analysis on a week of request samples and produce config suggestions.
[04:22] [04:25] Maya Chu: Any notes on quantization — we run Llama variants internally.
[04:29] Ethan Cole: For on-prem and Dedicated we recommend 4-bit quantization for Llama and you may see slight quality tradeoffs, we'll include sample evals. The runtime selects kernels based on quant profile — sometimes the transcriber shows 'kernel' as 'kernel l', but that's fine.
[04:47] [04:50] Samira Patel: Okay, quick live install. Ethan, walk through pip/npm install and a one-minute run.
[04:56] Ethan Cole: Commands: pip install redwood-inference-example (placeholder) then python quickstart.py. For TS: npm i @redwood/inference and run node quickstart.mjs.
[05:10] [05:12] [Ethan runs the sample, console logs appear with token counts and latency]
[05:20] Ethan Cole: You can see here the sample response, token breakdown printed by the SDK, and a small latency of ~180ms in this sandbox. In dedicated we'd expect lower tail latency depending on GPU choice.
[05:35] Lena Ortiz: That token breakdown is useful. Is cost per token shown in logs?
[05:39] Ethan Cole: Not in logs by default, but our console maps token usage to a cost metric per token and you can enable cost logging to emit per-request cost fields.
[05:48] [05:50] Rajesh Menon: We also need to control model rollouts — can we pin versions?
[05:54] Ethan Cole: Absolutely. You can pin model/version per route, and we support canary rollouts and automatic fallback when a model variant is unavailable.
[06:03] [06:06] Tom Becker: For the pilot, we're thinking of a UAT environment that needs private endpoints and stricter logs. How long to onboard Dedicated?
[06:12] Samira Patel: For Dedicated, typical lead time is 4-6 weeks depending on capacity and network approvals. Private on-prem can take longer. For the pilot we often start with Hosted + VPC peering to reduce risk.
[06:24] Maya Chu: Show of hands — are there any blockers from our side to start a small pilot?
[06:29] Lena Ortiz: Need to confirm compliance with our Data Protection Officer, but I think that's quick.
[06:32] Rajesh Menon: I'll circulate network egress and firewall rules.
[06:35] Diego Morales: Great — I'll add the SOC2 and encryption summary to the follow-up.
[06:40] [06:42] Ethan Cole: Quick demo of streaming in TS — showing chunked partial responses, and how to hook that into a websockets-based UI. Note: there's an example in the repo under 'realtime' but the README has an outdated URL, we updated it today though.
[06:58] [07:00] Lena Ortiz: Any gotchas for CI secrets? We use GitHub Actions, need best practices on secret rotation.
[07:05] Samira Patel: We recommend using short-lived tokens in CI with a credential exchange pattern and storing long-lived credentials in your vault. We'll link a sample GH Actions workflow.
[07:15] [07:18] Rajesh Menon: For the SSO mapping, can we scope to specific models? We only want the assistant to hit the curated model, not the big general model.
[07:24] Ethan Cole: Yes, model-level RBAC is supported — you can restrict routes to model IDs. We'll provide a sample policy snippet in the security guide.
[07:33] [07:36] Maya Chu: Great. On the cost front, if we hit spikes, any auto-fallback?
[07:40] Samira Patel: We have routing policies — you can fallback to cheaper quantized model variants or move traffic to a lower-cost region. For mission-critical flows you can set a priority to avoid fallback.
[07:52] [07:55] Tom Becker: One last infra question: if we do VPC peering, what's the authentication handshake?
[07:59] Diego Morales: It's standard mutual TLS plus token exchange. We'll share the network template and a small diagram.
[08:10] [08:12] Ethan Cole: Alright, final wrap — recap of what we’ll send: quickstart repo, sandbox creds, SOC2 summary, network IP ranges, example GH Actions, and an initial Optimize config suggestion request.
[08:26] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. Also please include an example of the batching config — we want to see the latency impact numbers.
[08:33] Samira Patel: Will do. Diego, Ethan — anything else to add?
[08:36] Diego Morales: I’ll add the compliance and SSO mapping docs.
[08:39] Ethan Cole: I’ll queue up a small benchmark using their sample payloads once Rajesh shares them.
[08:44] Maya Chu: Thanks, everyone. Looking forward.
[08:46] Samira Patel: Thanks — we’ll follow up with the links and set the pilot kickoff for next week if that works.
[08:51] [call ends]
questions: Does Redwood support short-lived tokens and token rotation?
How does batching affect tail latency for customer traffic?
What network egress is required for hosted deployments?
Can RBAC be mapped from Okta groups to model-level access?
